paras: The pursuit of Jim Williams near Plano was a manhunt in Collin County, Texas, on May 31, 1882, in which ten or twelve armed citizens chased a farm hand accused of attempted rape and said they would lynch him if they caught him. The only account, a Plano dispatch to the Dallas Herald, left him at large, and no report of his capture or death was found.

Williams worked as a hired hand on the farm of Henry Morrison, seven miles southeast of Plano, whom the correspondent called "one of our most respectable citizens." He owed Morrison a small sum for a horse he had bought and was riding.

According to the dispatch, Williams tried to rape Mrs. Morrison between 10 and 11 o'clock on the morning of May 30, while her husband was in Dallas on business. The correspondent wrote that he threw her on the bed and fled to the woods when a passing wagon alarmed him, after which she ran to nearby neighbors and told them what had happened.

On the morning of May 31 Williams came back to the house, by the dispatch's account to settle his debt with Morrison, found no one at home, and fled "for parts unknown." By then ten or twelve armed citizens were "in hot pursuit," and the correspondent reported that if caught he would get "a speedy trial before Judge Lynch."
No later report of Williams's capture, arrest, trial or lynching appears in the coverage, and no officer is mentioned in the pursuit.

The story ran as a brief "Special to the Herald" from Plano in the Dallas daily herald on June 1, 1882, beside other state specials, and the Dallas weekly herald reprinted the same text on June 8. The dispatch called Williams "the villain" with a "hellish purpose" and reported the planned lynching without comment, set among items on a saloon fight and a hailstorm. It did not state Williams's race, and no Black-press account exists for this period.
